newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Menem uses strike to display his power.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Menem uses strike to display his power.

text.p: Stung by allegations his authority is being challenged, Argentine President Carlos Menem is using the spotlight thrown on him by last week's general strike to show he is still very much in command.
In what was widely interpreted as a direct challenge to unions, Menem announced several unpopular economic reforms in the heat of the 36-hour strike, the second in 50 days.
"Obviously Menem wants to show that his political leadership is not in crisis," said leading political analyst Enrique Zuleta Puceiro. "He wants to do away with any doubts about his strength."

For weeks Menem has faced a barrage of criticism for "losing the initiative" -- when even his foes recognize that initiative was a distinctive trait of his first term from 1989-1995, when his reforms changed the face of the country.
During that period, Menem privatized most state companies, threw the country open to foreign competition, brought down hyperinflation to zero and fomented high levels of economic growth.
But a recession last year coupled with growing unemployment, currently at 17 percent, dampened the euphoria and sent Menem's public approval ratings crashing.

Having won a second term in office in May 1995 with 50 percent of the vote, two opinion polls conducted in September showed only 14 to 15 percent of Argentines had a good or very good impression of Menem's government.
Under siege from unions and growing public malaise, but also from international markets eager to see the president taking charge again, Menem took sides with the latter.
On the first day of the strike last Thursday, Menem defiantly announced the privatization of the state mortgage bank -- a sell-off opposed by unions -- and a hike in public transport fares.

Stoking the debate even more, in quick succession he then submitted a controversial labor reform bill to Congress in the face of fierce union opposition. He said he would deregulate labor-controlled healthcare plans, the unions' most prized asset since the days of Peronist Party founder Juan Peron.
Menem also ridiculed labor leaders by accusing them of staging a "tourist" strike just to enjoy a long weekend.

"Menem has sought to demonstrate that he still retains a large share of power," said political analyst Rosendo Fraga, recalling that Menem managed also to pass a fiscal austerity package opposed by unions just a week before the strike.

Some analysts say it is unclear if Menem will win the showdown with unions and continue pushing through reforms. Put on a war footing by Menem's move on their healthcare funds, they are already threatening another general strike, this time for 48 hours.
"So far he is doing fine. But if at any point he starts negotiating again with unions, they will give him the kiss of death," predicted one economic consultant.
